1373.title: The Thief Who Stole My Heart
1373.hook: a father finds milk on his small son's lips and demands to know who fed him
1373.carry: grace comes first: shiva steals the heart
1373.howItsDone: Sambandar's hymns are sung by oduvars, the singers of Tamil Shaiva temples, and the story of the milk at the temple tank is told at Sirkazhi, the town of his birth.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Appar sent a king a song instead of himself: namah shivaya, we belong to Shiva, not to fear.

segments.voice: Who gave you this milk? A father stands over his small son on the steps of a temple tank, and he's angry. He went down into the water to bathe and left the boy on the bank. Now he's come up, there's milk on the child's lips, and nobody else in sight. He raises a stick. Who fed you? The boy doesn't cry or make an excuse. He lifts his hand, points up at the sky, and starts to sing. Today, another of the Tevaram's three singers: Sambandar.
screen: `WHO GAVE YOU THIS MILK?` → `A SMALL BOY POINTS UP.` → `AND STARTS TO SING.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The town is Sirkazhi, in the Tamil country. While his father is under the water, the child, alone, cries out for his mother and father. Shiva and the Goddess appear above the tank. She fills a golden cup with her own milk, mixed with divine wisdom, and gives it to him. Then they're gone, and the father comes up the steps. The boy's song begins, in paraphrase: the one with an earring in his ear, who rides the bull, who wears the pure white crescent moon, smeared with the ash of the burning ground, he is the thief who stole my heart. He lives here, in this town. Asked who fed him, the boy gives a portrait, the way you'd describe someone you'd just seen up close. Then that phrase: the thief who stole my heart. A strange thing to call God, and a tender one. The boy didn't earn the milk. He cried, and it came. Shiva takes the heart first, and the song comes after. Tamil Shaivas have a word for this: arul, grace. God moves first; worship is the answer, not the price. And notice where the song ends: in this town, here. The Tevaram's hymns name their temples, and Tamil Shaivas still go on pilgrimage to the places they sing. His father came up the steps to scold him, and went home with a hymn.
screen: `A CHILD ALONE ON THE BANK` · `MILK IN A GOLDEN CUP` · `THE THIEF WHO STOLE MY HEART` · `ARUL: GRACE COMES FIRST`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what has stolen your heart lately, not what ought to have, but what actually did: a face, a piece of music, a view from a window. Notice that you didn't earn it. It came first, and you answered. If you pray, give one line back to God today, a thank-you or a verse, the way the boy sang back to Shiva. If you don't, say the thank-you to whoever brought it to you.

1374.title: Kannappa the Hunter
1374.hook: a hunter brings Shiva water carried in his mouth and meat he has tasted first
1374.carry: the heart is the real offering
1374.howItsDone: Kannappa is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and his story is told at the Shiva temple of Kalahasti, the hill shrine where tradition places it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sambandar, fed by the Goddess before he asked: grace comes first, and he sang of the thief who stole his heart.
screen: `GRACE COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Water, carried up a hill in a man's mouth, because he has no pot. Wildflowers tucked into his hair, because his hands are full. A piece of roasted meat, which he has bitten into first, to make sure it's tender and good. A young hunter climbs into a forest shrine and lays all this before Shiva. He spits the water over the stone to wash it, shakes the flowers from his hair, sets down the meat, and stands guard all night with his bow. Today, the hunter the Tamil Shaiva saints call Kannappa.
screen: `WATER CARRIED IN HIS MOUTH.` → `FLOWERS IN HIS HAIR.` → `MEAT HE TASTED FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The shrine already has a priest, a careful man who comes each morning with pure water and proper flowers. Each morning he finds the place littered with bones and wilted blossoms, grieves, cleans it all, and worships again. At last Shiva tells him: hide tomorrow, and watch. The hunter arrives and sees blood running from one eye of Shiva's image. Herbs don't stop it. So he takes an arrow, cuts out his own eye, and presses it to the place. The bleeding stops, and he laughs with joy. Then the other eye of the image begins to bleed. He sets his foot on it to mark the spot, and raises the arrow again. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and holds his hand. Stop, Kannappa. The story doesn't mock the priest. His worship was right. But Shiva lets him see a love that knew none of the rules and held nothing back. That's bhakti at its rawest: what God receives is the heart inside the offering. Krishna says it in the Gita too, in paraphrase: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water, offered with love, I accept. And Sundarar, in a hymn listing the Lord's servants, names the hunter among them. One thing, plainly: this is a story about love, not a model to copy, and Shiva himself stops the hand. If you ever feel pulled to hurt yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1375.title: Love Itself Is Shiva
1375.hook: love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know: Tirumular's short verse
1375.carry: anbe sivam: love itself is shiva
1375.tomorrow: The King, the Merchant and the Mother
1375.howItsDone: Tirumular is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and the words 'anbe sivam', love is Shiva, from his verse are spoken and written by Tamil Shaivas.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kannappa, the hunter who knew none of the rules: the heart is the real offering, and Shiva's own hand stopped him.
screen: `THE HEART IS THE REAL OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. That's the first line of a short Tamil verse, spoken by a man the tradition calls Tirumular. How he got that name is strange. A traveling yogi comes upon a herd of cows gathered around the body of their cowherd, who has just died. The cows are lowing, circling, refusing to leave him. The yogi can't bear it. So, the story says, he leaves his own body and enters the cowherd's. And the cowherd stands up.
screen: `COWS AROUND A DEAD COWHERD.` → `A YOGI CAN'T BEAR IT.` → `THE COWHERD STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest, as the Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The cows, comforted, go home. The yogi means to return to his own body, but when he looks for it, it's gone. Shiva's will, the story says. So he stays in the cowherd's body, under the cowherd's name, Mular, and settles down to meditate and compose the Tirumantiram, a long book of verses on Shiva and the path to him. It sits in the Tirumurai, the collection that holds the Tevaram. Now the verse, in paraphrase. Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. No one knows that love itself is Shiva. When they know that love itself is Shiva, they rest there, as love, as Shiva. The verse doesn't say Shiva is loving, the way you'd say a person is kind. It goes further: the love is Shiva. Not a quality he has, but who he is. Now go back to the field. The story starts with a man who couldn't bear the grief of some cows. He wasn't seeking a vision. He was moved by animals crying for their herder, and gave up his own body to comfort them. Before he wrote a single verse, he'd already done what the verse says. Looking back over these Tamil days: Appar, who belonged wholly to Shiva; Sambandar, whose heart was stolen; Kannappa, who held nothing back; and Tirumular, saying it plainly. Tamil Shaivas still write it in two words: anbe sivam, love is Shiva.
screen: `THE BODY HE COULDN'T FIND` · `THE TIRUMANTIRAM` · `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA` · `HE DID IT BEFORE HE WROTE IT`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a person or even an animal, see their face for a moment, and feel the warmth that comes with it. Then gently let the face fade and stay with the warmth, not the person now, just the love; when the mind goes looking for the face, let it, and come back. If you pray, rest in the verse's two words, anbe sivam. If you don't, just rest in the warmth.

1376.title: The King, the Merchant and the Mother
1376.hook: a king and a merchant, both thrown out, can't stop worrying about the people who did it
1376.carry: the mother who binds is the mother who frees
1376.howItsDone: In Bengal the Devi Mahatmya is known as the Chandi and is recited during Durga Puja; Shakta devotees call the Goddess Ma, while Vaishnava devotees gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of our Tamil Shaiva days: Tirumular, who comforted grieving cows, and anbe sivam, love itself is Shiva.
screen: `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Two men meet at a forest hermitage, and both have lost everything. One is a king, beaten by enemies and robbed by his own ministers. The other is a merchant, thrown out of his house by his own wife and sons, who wanted his money. And here's the strange thing: neither can stop worrying about the people who threw him out. Is my treasury safe? Are my sons all right? Today we cross to Bengal, and open the Goddess's best-loved book.
screen: `A KING WHO LOST HIS KINGDOM.` → `A MERCHANT THROWN OUT BY HIS SONS.` → `NEITHER CAN LET GO.`

segments.voice: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, and it opens with these two. The king is Suratha, the merchant Samadhi, and they put their question to the sage of the hermitage, Medhas. We know these people wronged us. So why does the mind keep running back to them? The sage answers: look at the birds. Hungry themselves, they still drop grain into their chicks' beaks. Even the wise get pulled like that, by a great power, Mahamaya, the Goddess herself. She binds the world in attachment, and when she's pleased, she's the one who sets it free. Then he tells them her stories, which fill the rest of the book: the Goddess rising when the gods can't win, her battles, and her promise that whenever trouble comes, she'll come again. And the two men? On a riverbank they shape an image of the Goddess out of earth and worship her for three years. She appears and asks what they want. The king asks for his kingdom back, and gets it. The merchant asks for something else: the knowledge that frees him from I and mine. He gets that. Here's the Shakta teaching, plainly: God as Shakti, the power that makes and moves everything, and for Shaktas, the Mother. The same power that ties the knot is the one you ask to untie it. In Bengal this book is called the Chandi, and it's recited at Durga Puja every autumn. So when an old hurt keeps replaying, a Shakta doesn't call it weakness. It's the Mother's power at work, and she's the one to ask.
screen: `WHY CAN'T WE LET GO?` · `MAHAMAYA: THE POWER THAT BINDS` · `AN IMAGE OF EARTH BY THE RIVER` · `THE MOTHER WHO BINDS IS THE MOTHER WHO FREES`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you keep replaying, someone who hurt you or let you down. Don't argue with them in your head; just notice the pull, the way the king and the merchant noticed theirs. Then do what Shakta devotees do: call her by her simplest name. On each out-breath, say Ma, and ask her to loosen the knot. If you don't pray, simply let each breath loosen your grip a little.

1377.title: Ramprasad's Ledger
1377.hook: a clerk's account book fills up with songs to Kali
1377.carry: god as ma: a child may bring her anything
1377.tomorrow: Humbler Than a Blade of Grass
1377.howItsDone: Ramprasad's songs to Kali are sung in Bengal at Kali Puja, at home and in devotional gatherings, as part of the song tradition known as Shyama Sangeet.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king and a merchant learned that the Mother who binds is the Mother who frees.
screen: `THE MOTHER WHO BINDS AND FREES.`

segments.voice: An office in Calcutta. A young clerk is supposed to be copying figures into the account book, rows of numbers, day after day. But the other clerks notice the margins of his ledger filling up with something else: lines of verse, songs to Kali, the dark Mother. Somebody takes the book to the employer, expecting the young man to be fired. The employer opens it, starts reading, and doesn't stop. Today, the Shakta stream through one singer: Ramprasad Sen.
screen: `A CLERK AND HIS LEDGER.` → `SONGS IN THE MARGINS.` → `THE EMPLOYER READS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the employer was so moved that instead of dismissing him, he sent Ramprasad home to his village with an allowance, so he could do nothing but sing. His songs spread from village to village, and tradition gives a melody his name. Listen to how he talks to Kali. Not like a courtier bowing to a queen. Like a child to his mother. In one song, in paraphrase, he complains: other children have a mother who looks after them, so why am I left like this? Is this how a mother behaves? He sulks, he pleads, he threatens to tell everyone. That's the Shakta teaching at its warmest: God as Ma. The Goddess may be fierce, with a sword and a necklace of heads, but to her child she is Mother, and a child may bring her anything, even a complaint. People tell a story about him. He was mending a fence and needed someone to hold the rope on the other side. His young daughter came and held it. Later, when he thanked her, she said she'd been away the whole time. So who held the rope? In the story, the Mother herself, wearing a little girl's face. And his songs aren't only sweet. In one, he scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer: this human life is a good field, and you've left it lying fallow. Tend it, and gold would grow. Tender with the Mother, hard on himself. That's the voice that came out of an account book.

1378.title: Humbler Than a Blade of Grass
1378.hook: a grammar teacher comes home from pilgrimage and every word he explains turns into Krishna
1378.carry: kirtan: the name, sung humbler than grass
1378.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who follow Chaitanya, gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to the khol drum and hand cymbals, and some take the singing into the streets.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramprasad, the clerk with songs in his ledger: god as Ma, and a child may bring her anything.
screen: `A CHILD MAY BRING HER ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: What happens to a grammar lesson when the teacher can only think of God? In Nabadwip, a town of scholars on the river, the teacher is young and sharp, known for his skill in Sanskrit grammar, and his students are proud to study with him. Then he goes away on a pilgrimage, and comes back different. He sits down to explain an ordinary word, a verb, a root, and somehow the explanation ends in Krishna. The next word, the same. The students look at each other. They came for grammar. Today, the Vaishnava stream, and a teacher you met earlier on this path: Chaitanya.
screen: `A YOUNG GRAMMAR TEACHER.` → `A PILGRIMAGE.` → `EVERY WORD ENDS IN KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: The biographies tell this story, and they don't make fun of the students. In the end he closes the school. He can't teach grammar anymore, because every word has become a door to the same room. So what does he do instead? He sings. With friends, in a courtyard at first, then out in the streets of Nabadwip: the names of God, Hari, Krishna, over and over to drums and cymbals, louder and faster, until people are dancing. That's kirtan, and in this stream it isn't decoration. It is the practice: the name, sung out loud, in company. The singing could sound like showing off. But Chaitanya is remembered for a handful of short teaching verses, and one of them, in paraphrase, says how to sing: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor to others and wanting none for yourself. A tree, the old explanation goes, gives shade even to the one who cuts it down. So the loudest practice in the stream is meant to come from the lowest place. Remember the conch on Bengal's first day, the Goddess as Mother? The Vaishnava stream also reaches for a close name. For Chaitanya's followers the closest of all is Radha's love for Krishna, and in their stories Chaitanya himself weeps and longs for Krishna the way Radha does. The scholar who couldn't stop saying Krishna ends up singing in the street, as low as grass.
screen: `EVERY WORD BECOMES KRISHNA` · `THE NAME, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS` · `LONGING LIKE RADHA`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, picture a blade of grass, low, bending when it's walked on, standing up again; on the out-breath, a tree, rooted, patient, giving shade. Go back and forth, grass and tree, and bring to mind one person who might need you to bend, or to wait. If you pray, let a name of God, Hari or Krishna or your own, sound softly with the breath.

1379.title: Durga Comes Home
1379.hook: a goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter, and sent back to the river
1379.carry: the goddess comes home as a daughter
1379.howItsDone: At Durga Puja, Bengali Hindus install clay images of Durga in homes and neighborhood pavilions, worship her for the festival days, and on Vijaya Dashami immerse the image in a river or pond.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaitanya and kirtan: the name, sung humbler than a blade of grass.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS.`

segments.voice: Straw, bound tight with twine into the shape of a body. Then clay from the riverbank, pressed on in layers, smoothed by thumbs, left to dry, cracked, filled, smoothed again, in workshops along the river in Bengal. Slowly a face appears: wide eyes, a calm mouth, many arms, a lion at her feet. Then paint, cloth, jewelry. By autumn she's ready, and families and neighborhoods carry her in. Today, the Shakta stream at its most public, Durga Puja, and what happens to her at the end.
screen: `STRAW AND RIVER CLAY.` → `A FACE APPEARS.` → `CARRIED IN, IN AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The text behind Durga is the Devi Mahatmya, and it tells of her as a warrior: the gods pour their powers into her, she rides out on her lion, and defeats the buffalo demon none of them could. That's the image in the clay, spear in hand. But in Bengal the festival tells a second story at the same time. Durga is also Uma, daughter of the mountain king Himalaya and his wife Menaka. She's married to Shiva and lives far away on his mountain, and once a year she comes home to visit her parents, bringing her children. So the festival feels like a homecoming. Bengali songs called agamani, songs of arrival, put words in the mother's mouth: is my Uma really coming? How thin has she gotten? What has that husband of hers been feeding her? In Bengal, the fierce goddess and the daughter whose mother worries are one. On the last day, Vijaya, she has to go back. Married women, in a custom called sindur khela, smear red vermilion on the goddess's face and on each other, the way you'd send a daughter off. Then the image, all that patient work, is carried to the river and lowered into the water, and the clay goes back where it came from. It's the same move as Ganesha's clay: the divine invited into an image, honored, and given back. The goodbye is sad; afterward people visit, embrace, share sweets. Behind us this week: Sambandar's song, Kannappa's eye, Tirumular's cows, the king and the merchant, Ramprasad's ledger, Chaitanya's street. Now a goddess who comes home, and goes.
screen: `THE WARRIOR ON THE LION` · `UMA, THE DAUGHTER COMING HOME` · `RED VERMILION FOR GOODBYE` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE RIVER`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, think of someone you love arriving, the door opening, their face, and let yourself be glad. On the out-breath, think of letting them go again, the door closing, the car pulling away, and hold on to neither, just breathing the arriving and the leaving. If you pray, you can hold that person before the Goddess, or before God, as they come and as they go.
